_comment_file: The import wizard: eight steps that read an mRemoteNG, OpenSSH config or CSV file and write it into the vault. Loaded only when the wizard is opened. Two themes run through this namespace and neither may be softened in translation: nothing is written to the vault until step 7, and an import cannot be undone once it is. 'Remoter' is the product name and is never translated. 'mRemoteNG', 'ProxyJump', 'ProxyCommand', 'Host', 'Match', 'confVersion', 'AES-CBC' and 'MD5' are names from other products, protocols and file formats and are never translated either.

wizard._comment_title: The screen's heading. A noun — the name of the screen — not the verb on a button.
wizard.title: Import
wizard._comment_closeHint: Tooltip on the same button. 'Esc' is a key name and is written as-is in every language.

firstRun._comment_: Copy for the launch screen's import door and the vault creation it has to pass through on the way here. It lives in the import namespace rather than in vault.json because it describes the import flow and has to stay in step with the wizard's wording: the sentence it replaced was a stub promising the wizard 'in a later version', and the door it sat under led to the create-vault wizard and nowhere else.
firstRun._comment_doorHelp: Under 'Bring across what I have' on the first-run screen. It names what happens in order, because a door that creates a vault when you asked it to import reads as the wrong button. mRemoteNG, CSV and ~/.ssh/config are a product name, a file format and a file path; none of them is translated.
firstRun.doorHelp: A vault has to exist first, so this creates one — then opens the import wizard for mRemoteNG, ~/.ssh/config and CSV.
firstRun._comment_calloutTitle: Shown at the top of the create-vault wizard when the user arrived through the import door. Short: it is a reassurance, not an instruction.
firstRun._comment_calloutBody: The body under it. 'Nothing is read until then' is the same promise the wizard's own footer makes and must not be softened.
firstRun.calloutBody: Finish these four steps and the import wizard opens on the other side. Nothing from your old connection manager is read until then.
firstRun._comment_openAndImport: The last button of vault creation, replacing 'I have saved it — open the vault' when the import wizard follows it. It still confirms the recovery key has been saved: that confirmation is the whole point of the screen and must not be dropped in translation.
firstRun.openAndImport: I have saved it — start the import

rail._comment_: The eight-step progress rail down the top of the screen. Each label is one or two words in a narrow button, and each is a noun naming the step, not an instruction. Steps 3 and 7 are work the wizard does by itself; they are in the rail so the wait has a place on screen.
rail.label: Import steps

step._comment_secrets: The document password, and what the file's own protection turned out to be.
step._comment_parse: Reading the file. A noun here: the name of the step, not the imperative 'parse it'.
step._comment_report: What the parse found — the findings list.
step._comment_destination: The vault folder the import lands in.
step._comment_commit: Writing to the vault. A noun: the name of the step.

nav._comment_: The forward and back buttons in the footer. Imperative verbs, no trailing punctuation. Which forward label is shown depends on the step.
nav._comment_detect: Step 1, before the file has been looked at: pressing this reads the file's header to work out what it is. It does not parse it and it does not write anything.
nav._comment_parse: Step 2: pressing this parses the whole file into a preview. Still writes nothing.
nav._comment_toCommit: Moves to the last step before anything is written, where the user presses the button that writes.

footer._comment_: A standing note at the bottom of every step, saying whether the vault has been touched. SECURITY-CRITICAL: these three sentences are the wizard's promise about when it writes. Do not merge them, do not soften 'yet', and do not turn the warning into a reassurance.
footer.nothingWritten: Nothing has been written to your vault yet.
footer.willWrite: This step writes to your vault.

gate._comment_: Why a disabled control is disabled. Each is a tooltip on the control itself, so it says what to do rather than what went wrong. Every one is a complete sentence.
gate.noFile: Choose the file you want to import.
gate.unknownFormat: Remoter could not tell what this file is. Choose the format yourself.
gate.noPassword: This file needs its document password before it can be read.
gate._comment_nothingTicked: 'Ticked' throughout this namespace means the checkbox beside a node in the preview tree. Use whatever word your language uses for a checked checkbox.
gate.nothingTicked: Everything is unticked. Tick at least one item to import.
gate.committed: This import has already been written. Start another one to import again.
gate.ahead: Finish the steps before this one first.

source._comment_: Step 1 — choosing the file. Detection is done by reading the file's content, never its name.
source.title: Choose the file to import
source.lead: Remoter reads the file to work out what it is. Nothing is written to your vault until you commit, and the parse runs in the core, not in this window.
source._comment_browsing: The same button while the operating system's file dialog is opening.
source._comment_dialogTitle: The title of the operating system's own file-picker window.
source.dialogFailed: The system file dialog did not open. Type the path instead.
source._comment_pathLabel: Accessible name of the text field the path is typed into.
source._comment_pathPlaceholder: An example file path, shown greyed out in the empty field. A path, not prose: translate nothing but the placeholder user name if your language's convention differs.
source.noFileHint: Choose a file, or type its path.
source._comment_puttyLocal: A button under the path field. PuTTY keeps its saved sessions in the Windows registry or in ~/.putty/sessions, where no file dialog would find them; this fills the path in.
source.puttyNone: No saved PuTTY sessions were found on this computer.
source.detectFailed: That file could not be read.
source._comment_detectedAs: {label} is the format's name, from the core — 'mRemoteNG 1.77', 'OpenSSH config'. Never translated.
source._comment_chosenAs: Same {label}, but the user overruled detection. The distinction matters: one is what the file says it is, the other is what the user says it is.
source.unknownTitle: Remoter does not recognise this file
source.unknownBody: Nothing in it matched a format this build can read. If you know what it is, choose it below and Remoter will parse it as that. If it parses into nonsense, nothing is lost: the preview is where you would see it, and the preview writes nothing.
source.needsPassword: This file is encrypted. The next step asks for its password.
source.noPassword: No document password is needed for this file.
source._comment_formatLabel: Heading and accessible name of the radio group below it. 'Parse it as' — the user is telling Remoter which reader to use.

format._comment_: The importers this build has. The labels are product and format names and are never translated; the hints under them are copy and are. Each hint names the file a user would recognise.
format.archiveHint: .rmtr, exported from Remoter with its passwords
format.jsonHint: A JSON export from Remoter: the tree, without passwords
format.mremotengHint: confCons.xml, with or without a document password
format.rdcmanHint: .rdg — groups, servers and accounts; saved passwords stay with Windows
format._comment_rdpFileHint: '.rdp' is a file extension and is never translated. 'Windows' keeps the saved password because Windows encrypted it for one account.
format.rdpFileHint: .rdp — one connection per file; a saved password stays with Windows
format._comment_puttyHint: 'reg' is the Windows command that exports registry keys, and '~/.putty/sessions' a path; neither is translated.
format.puttyHint: Saved sessions: this computer's, a reg export, or ~/.putty/sessions
format._comment_sshConfigHint: 'ProxyJump' and 'Include' are OpenSSH configuration keywords and are never translated.
format.csvHint: A header row and one connection per line

secrets._comment_: Step 2 — the document password, and the bad news that arrives with it. The password is typed here, handed to the core, and dropped. It is never shown, never stored and never logged.
secrets.encryptedLead: Remoter needs the document password to read the credentials inside. The parse happens in the core, in a sandboxed reader; nothing is written to your vault until you commit.
secrets._comment_plainTitle: Shown instead when the file needs no password: there is nothing for the user to type on this step.
secrets.plainLead: This file needs no password. The next step reads it and shows you the tree it would create.
secrets._comment_archiveTitle: Shown instead when the file is a Remoter archive (.rmtr). The password is the one chosen at export in Remoter — NOT the vault password and NOT another application's document password.
secrets.archiveLead: Remoter needs the password this archive was exported with. It opens the connections and the server passwords inside; nothing is written to your vault until you commit.
secrets.archivePasswordHelp: The password chosen when this archive was exported. Not your vault password.
secrets._comment_passwordLabel: The password that protects the file being imported — NOT the user's vault password. Keep that distinction visible in translation.
secrets.passwordHelp: The password mRemoteNG asks for when it opens this file.
secrets._comment_show: Verb, on the button that reveals the typed password as plain text.
secrets._comment_hide: Verb, on the same button once the password is revealed.
secrets.parseFailed: That file could not be read.
secrets._comment_formatChosen: Sits where the detected format's name would be, when detection failed and the user picked the format instead.
secrets._comment_confVersion: 'confVersion' is the mRemoteNG document's own version field and is never translated. {version} is its value, e.g. '2.6'.
secrets._comment_defaultTitle: SECURITY-CRITICAL. mRemoteNG encrypts a file that has no password of its own with a password published in its own source code, so such a file protects nothing. This must not be softened into 'this file has no password': the user believed it was protected and is entitled to learn plainly that it was not.
secrets.defaultTitle: This file was not really protected
secrets._comment_defaultBody: SECURITY-CRITICAL. Same as above. 'Anyone who has ever held a copy' is the point of the sentence; do not reduce it to a possibility.
secrets.defaultBody: It carries no password of its own. mRemoteNG encrypts such files with a password published in its own source, so anyone who has ever held a copy of this file could read every credential in it. The report after the parse will confirm what was found.
secrets._comment_legacyTitle: SECURITY-CRITICAL. The pre-1.75 mRemoteNG scheme: an unsalted MD5 of the password for a key, and ciphertext nothing could detect tampering in. 'AES-CBC' and 'MD5' are algorithm names and are never translated.
secrets.legacyTitle: This file uses legacy AES-CBC with an MD5-derived key
secrets._comment_legacyBody: SECURITY-CRITICAL. The instruction to change the passwords on the servers is the actionable part and must survive translation.
secrets.legacyBody: Remoter can read it. You should know that anyone who has had a copy of this file could have read it too, without much effort. Consider the credentials inside it exposed and change them on the servers after the import.
secrets.fullFileBody: Not just the passwords — the structure too. Nothing changes about the import; it tells you how the file was configured.
secrets._comment_keysTitle: 'Keys' here means private keys — SSH key files — not keyboard keys and not vault key slots.
secrets.keysBody: Keys named by this file are imported as references to the files they already live in. Remoter does not read the key material here, so no key passphrase is asked for.

parse._comment_: Step 3 — the wait while the core reads the file. The user does nothing here.
parse.busyNote: The parse runs in the core, in a sandboxed reader with bounded buffers. Nothing is written to your vault by it.

preview._comment_: Step 4 — every node the import would create, with a checkbox beside it. This is the last screen on which anything can be left out.
preview.title: This is what you will get
preview.lead: Nothing has been written yet. Untick anything you do not want.
preview._comment_countConnections: Label under a large number in a stat tile. A plain noun, lower case, no number in it.
preview._comment_countAttention: Label under the count of findings rated warning or alert — the ones the user may have to act on.
preview.treeHead: Tree as it will be created
preview._comment_treeNote: A fragment beside the heading, not a sentence: the folder structure and the inherited settings arrive as they were in the file.
preview._comment_filter: Placeholder and accessible name of the box that filters the tree. 'user' here is the account name on a connection.
preview.filter: Filter by name, host or user
preview._comment_ticked: {included} of {total} checkboxes are still ticked. Both are numbers.
preview.attentionNone: The parse found nothing that needs a decision from you.
preview._comment_attentionMore: Sits under a short list of findings, when more of them are on the report step. English's two branches are identical; the plural is here because most other languages inflect 'more' or need a different form after certain numbers.
preview.attentionMore: {count, plural, one {# more on the next step.} other {# more on the next step.}}
preview._comment_cleanHead: The opposite list: what the importer mapped without any loss.
preview.cleanFolders: {count, plural, one {# folder with its inheritance} other {# folders with their inheritance}}
preview._comment_cleanCredentials: A credential object is one stored username-and-secret that several connections can share.
preview.cleanCredentials: {count, plural, one {# credential object and its links} other {# credential objects and their links}}
preview._comment_cleanGateways: A jump host is an intermediate server a connection is made through. ProxyJump is the OpenSSH keyword that names one and is never translated.
preview.cleanGateways: {count, plural, one {# jump-host chain from ProxyJump, wired up as a real gateway} other {# jump-host chains from ProxyJump, wired up as real gateways}}
preview.cleanSecrets: {count, plural, one {# password to seal into the vault on commit} other {# passwords to seal into the vault on commit}}
preview._comment_conflictsTitle: SECURITY-ADJACENT, and the most easily misread thing on the screen: Remoter does not compare the import against the vault, so a name that already exists arrives twice. Do not translate this into a promise that duplicates are handled.
preview.conflictsTitle: Remoter will not merge with what is already there
preview.conflictsBody: This import cannot compare itself against your vault, so anything whose name already exists arrives as a second copy beside the first. Untick it here — that is the only place it can be stopped, because an import cannot be undone once it is committed.
preview.truncatedTitle: This is not the whole file
preview.truncatedBody: A safety limit stopped the parse before the end of the document. What you see is everything Remoter read, and importing it is safe; it will not be everything the file contains.

tree._comment_: The preview tree itself: one row per node, each with a checkbox and small badges.
tree._comment_group: Accessible name of the whole tree, read by a screen reader on entering it.
tree._comment_expandNode: Accessible name of the triangle beside a folder. {name} is the node's own name, in whatever script the user wrote it.
tree._comment_gateway: A badge on a row, not a sentence. {hops} is how many jump hosts the connection goes through; the multiplication sign is deliberate and reads as 'times'.
tree._comment_gatewayTitle: The badge's tooltip, saying in words what the badge says in a number. {count} is the same hop count.
tree.gatewayTitle: {count, plural, one {A jump-host chain of # hop came across with this connection.} other {A jump-host chain of # hops came across with this connection.}}
tree._comment_kept: A badge counting settings that had no equivalent in Remoter's data model and were preserved verbatim instead of dropped. Short: it sits in a row of badges.
tree.keptTitle: {count, plural, one {# setting with no equivalent here, preserved verbatim in custom fields.} other {# settings with no equivalent here, preserved verbatim in custom fields.}}
tree._comment_secret: A badge, lower case: this node brings a password with it.
tree.secretTitle: A password from the file will be sealed into the vault for this node.
tree._comment_inherited: A badge: this node has no credential of its own and uses its parent's, exactly as it did in the file.
tree.inheritedTitle: This node's credential comes from its parent, as it did in the file.

report._comment_: Step 5 — the findings, grouped by severity, worst first.
report.title: What the parse found
report.lead: Read this before you commit. Everything on it is still changeable — the preview is one step back, and nothing has been written.
report._comment_countFolders: Labels under the large numbers in the stat tiles. Plain nouns and noun phrases, lower case.
report._comment_countSecrets: Passwords the importer got out of the file. Not yet in the vault at this point.
report._comment_countSkipped: Items the parser could not use at all. Distinct from the ones the user unticks.
report._comment_groupAlerts: Heading over the findings the user has to do something about. Imperative.
report._comment_groupWarnings: Heading over findings that change nothing but that the user should know.
report._comment_groupInfo: Heading over findings kept purely so the import can be accounted for afterwards.
report.none: Nothing to report. The file mapped cleanly.
report._comment_preservedHead: The section listing settings that had no equivalent in Remoter and were stored verbatim rather than dropped.
report.preservedNote: Nothing was discarded. If a later version of Remoter learns to read these, they will be there.
report.skippedTitle: Some items were left out by the parser
report.skippedBody: They are listed above with the reason. They are not in the preview and will not be imported; the file itself is untouched, so nothing about them is lost.

preserved._comment_: One line each in the 'kept but not interpreted' table. The left column is a field path — 'custom_fields.ProxyCommand' — and is never translated; these are the right column. 'verbatim' means the value was stored exactly as the file had it.
preserved.connections: {count, plural, one {# connection} other {# connections}} · verbatim
preserved.settings: {count, plural, one {# setting} other {# settings}} on {items, plural, one {# item} other {# items}} · verbatim
preserved._comment_everyRow: For a CSV column: every row of the file carried it.

finding._comment_: One entry per thing the importer wants the user to know. Each has a title — the fact — and a body saying what it means for them. A verbatim scrap from the file is shown separately in a monospace line and is never translated. {item} is a connection or folder name from the file; {target}, {protocol}, {command}, {column}, {field}, {criteria} and {pattern} are all values read out of the file, in whatever script or syntax it had them.
finding._comment_defaultFilePasswordTitle: SECURITY-CRITICAL. The single most important finding in the wizard. mRemoteNG encrypts a file with no password of its own using a password published in its own source. Do not soften 'was not really protected' and do not turn 'change them on the servers' into a suggestion.
finding.defaultFilePasswordTitle: This file was protected with mRemoteNG's well-known default password.
finding.defaultFilePasswordBody: It was not really protected. Anyone who has ever held a copy of it could read every credential inside without knowing anything you know. Treat the passwords coming across as exposed and change them on the servers.
finding._comment_legacyCbcEncryptionTitle: SECURITY-CRITICAL. The pre-1.75 scheme: the key was an unsalted MD5 hash of the password and the ciphertext was unauthenticated. 'Consider the credentials exposed' is the actionable part.
finding.legacyCbcEncryptionTitle: This file uses the legacy AES-CBC scheme with an MD5-derived key.
finding.legacyCbcEncryptionBody: Remoter can read it. So could anyone else with a copy, without much effort, because the key came from an unsalted hash and the ciphertext carried nothing to detect tampering. Consider the credentials inside it exposed.
finding.fullFileEncryptionTitle: The whole document was encrypted, not just its passwords.
finding.fullFileEncryptionBody: The structure was hidden as well as the credentials. Nothing changes about the import; it is noted because it tells you how the file was configured.
finding._comment_secretsRecoveredTitle: How many passwords the importer got out of the file.
finding.secretsRecoveredTitle: {count, plural, one {# password came out of the file.} other {# passwords came out of the file.}}
finding.secretsRecoveredBody: They are sealed into the vault at the moment you commit. They are never written to disk in the clear and never leave the core.
finding._comment_secretsNotCarriedTitle: A Remoter JSON export names which kind of secret each credential holds and never carries the secret, so these credentials arrive and ask for their password or key when first used. {count} is how many.
finding.secretsNotCarriedTitle: {count, plural, one {# credential arrives without its password or key.} other {# credentials arrive without their passwords or keys.}}
finding.secretsNotCarriedBody: A JSON export records which kind of secret each credential holds, never the secret. They come in as they were, and each asks for its password or key the first time it is used.
finding._comment_protectedPasswordsNotCarriedTit: Passwords saved by Remote Desktop Connection or Remote Desktop Connection Manager are encrypted by Windows (DPAPI) for the account that saved them, so no other account or computer can read them. {count} is how many.
finding.protectedPasswordsNotCarriedTitle: {count, plural, one {# saved password stays behind with Windows.} other {# saved passwords stay behind with Windows.}}
finding.protectedPasswordsNotCarriedBody: Windows encrypted them for the account that saved them, and only that account on that computer can read them. The credentials come in with their user names, and each asks for its password the first time it is used.
finding._comment_rdGatewayNotSupportedTitle: 'Remote Desktop Gateway' is Microsoft's product; use the name Windows uses for it in this language. The gateway's address is shown beneath in a monospace line.
finding.rdGatewayNotSupportedTitle: {item} goes through a Remote Desktop Gateway.
finding.rdGatewayNotSupportedBody: Remoter cannot connect through a Remote Desktop Gateway yet, so it will try to reach the server directly. The gateway's address is kept with the connection.
finding._comment_proxyNotSupportedTitle: A PuTTY session set to reach its server through a SOCKS, HTTP or Telnet proxy or a local command. The proxy's kind and address are shown beneath in a monospace line.
finding.proxyNotSupportedTitle: {item} goes through a proxy Remoter does not use.
finding.proxyNotSupportedBody: Remoter will connect to it directly. The proxy's settings are kept with the connection, but never its password.
finding._comment_credentialProfileMissingTitle: {profile} is the name of a credential profile in Remote Desktop Connection Manager. 'Remote Desktop Connection Manager' is a product name and is never translated.
finding.credentialProfileMissingTitle: {item} uses the credential profile {profile}, which is not in the file.
finding.credentialProfileMissingBody: Remote Desktop Connection Manager keeps that kind of profile on the computer that wrote the file. An empty credential named after it takes its place: fill in the user name, and the password is asked for the first time it is used.
finding._comment_credentialsDeduplicatedTitle: The same username and password repeated across many connections became one shared credential. {credentials} counts the credential objects made, {connections} the connections now pointing at them.
finding.credentialsDeduplicatedTitle: {credentials, plural, one {# credential object covers} other {# credential objects cover}} {connections, plural, one {# connection} other {# connections}}.
finding.credentialsDeduplicatedBody: The same username and password repeated across connections became one credential each, linked from the connections that used it. Changing it once now changes it everywhere.
finding._comment_unknownProtocolTitle: {item} is the connection's name. The protocol name itself is shown separately and is never translated.
finding.unknownProtocolTitle: {item} used a protocol Remoter does not have.
finding._comment_unknownProtocolBody: {mappedTo} is the protocol it was imported as — SSH, RDP, VNC, SFTP. Never translated.
finding.unknownProtocolBody: It was imported as {mappedTo}. The original value is kept in a custom field, so nothing about it is lost.
finding._comment_skippedItemBody: One sentence per reason the parser refused an item. The reason names are wire values from the core and must stay exactly as they are; only the sentences are translated. 'other' is the fallback for a reason a newer core sends that this build has never seen.
finding.skippedItemBody: {reason, select, unusable_host {It was left out because its host name was not usable.} unusable_name {It was left out because its name was empty or not usable.} unsupported_kind {It was left out because its type has no equivalent here.} empty {It was left out because it was empty.} other {It was left out.}}
finding._comment_unmappedProxyCommandTitle: 'ProxyCommand' is an OpenSSH configuration keyword and is never translated.
finding.unmappedProxyCommandTitle: {item} uses a ProxyCommand that has no direct equivalent.
finding.unmappedProxyCommandBody: The command is kept verbatim in a custom field rather than dropped. The connection will import; it will not use the proxy until you wire up a gateway for it by hand.
finding._comment_gatewayMappedTitle: The best news the importer has: a ProxyJump in the file became a real, working chain of gateways in the vault.
finding.gatewayMappedTitle: {item} arrives with its jump-host chain intact.
finding.gatewayMappedBody: ProxyJump became a real gateway chain of {hops, plural, one {# hop} other {# hops}}, so the connection works from the first attempt without any further setup.
finding.gatewaySynthesisedTitle: A gateway for {item} was created from its jump host setting.
finding._comment_gatewaySynthesisedBody: {target} is the jump host's address, read out of the file.
finding.gatewaySynthesisedBody: The jump host {target} was not a connection in the file, so it became one here and is now shared by everything that jumps through it.
finding.gatewayUnresolvedTitle: {item} jumps through a host that could not be resolved.
finding.gatewayUnresolvedBody: The chain names {target}, which is not in the file and could not be built from it. The connection imports without its gateway and will not reach the host until you add one.
finding._comment_secretNotMappedTitle: SECURITY-ADJACENT. A password in a field Remoter has no home for. It was dropped rather than written somewhere unprotected, and the user is told so plainly because they may be relying on it.
finding.secretNotMappedTitle: A secret on {item} had nowhere to go.
finding.secretNotMappedBody: It was in a field the domain model has no home for, and a secret is the one thing that is never kept in a custom field. It was dropped rather than stored somewhere it would not be protected.
finding._comment_matchBlockNotAppliedTitle: 'Match' is an OpenSSH configuration keyword — a conditional block — and is never translated.
finding.matchBlockNotAppliedTitle: A Match block was read but not applied.
finding.matchBlockNotAppliedBody: Its criteria depend on how the connection is being made, which is not known at import time, so its {options, plural, one {# option was} other {# options were}} left out rather than applied to hosts they may not be meant for.
finding._comment_patternBlockAppliedTitle: 'Host' is the OpenSSH keyword that opens a block, and a wildcard one — 'Host *.acme' — applies to every matching connection. Never translated.
finding.patternBlockAppliedTitle: A wildcard Host block was applied to {connections, plural, one {# connection} other {# connections}}.
finding.patternBlockAppliedBody: Its options were folded into every connection whose name it matched, the same way ssh itself would apply them.
finding._comment_settingsPreservedTitle: Settings with no equivalent in Remoter, stored verbatim in custom fields instead of being dropped.
finding.settingsPreservedTitle: {count, plural, one {# setting on {item} was kept but not interpreted.} other {# settings on {item} were kept but not interpreted.}}
finding.settingsPreservedBody: They are in custom fields, verbatim. Nothing was discarded — if a later version of Remoter learns to read them, they will be there.
finding._comment_unknownColumnTitle: CSV only: a column heading the importer has no field for.
finding.unknownColumnTitle: A column in the file was not recognised.
finding.unknownColumnBody: Its values were kept in a custom field on each row rather than thrown away.
finding._comment_limitReachedTitle: A parse limit stopped the read before the end of the file. The limit names are wire values from the core and must stay exactly as they are; only the sentences around them are translated.
finding.limitReachedTitle: {limit, select, custom_fields {A safety limit stopped the parse: too many custom fields.} findings {A safety limit stopped the parse: too many findings.} nodes {A safety limit stopped the parse: too many nodes.} other {A safety limit stopped the parse.}}
finding.limitReachedBody: What you see is everything Remoter read before the limit. Importing it is safe; it will not be the whole file. Split the file, or import it in parts.
finding._comment_unknownTitle: Shown when a newer core reports a finding this build has never heard of. It is deliberately honest about being unable to explain itself rather than inventing a meaning.
finding.unknownTitle: This file produced a note this version does not recognise.
finding.unknownBody: It came from a newer part of the importer than this build knows about. Nothing is wrong with your file; the note simply cannot be explained here.

destination._comment_: Step 6 — the vault folder the import lands in.
destination.title: Where should this go?
destination.lead: Everything ticked in the preview is created under the folder you choose here, keeping the structure the file had.
destination._comment_topOption: The choice that puts the import at the root of the vault rather than inside any folder. This one stands on its own as a row in a list of folders.
destination.topOption: The top level of the vault
destination._comment_top: The same idea, but dropped into a sentence on the two steps after this one — 'Into the top level of the vault', 'Written into the top level of the vault as one transaction'. Lower case, and phrased so it reads as the object of a verb.
destination.top: the top level of the vault
destination.loadFailed: The vault's folders could not be read.
destination.noFolders: This vault has no folders yet. The import lands at the top level, keeping its own structure.
destination._comment_advice: The reason a folder of its own is recommended. Not a rule, and phrased as advice — but the reason behind it, that a commit cannot be undone, must survive translation.
destination.advice: A folder of its own is the safest choice. Remoter cannot undo a commit, and an import you can see in one place is an import you can delete in one action if it is not what you wanted.
destination._comment_chooseLabel: Accessible name of the list of folders.

conflicts._comment_: Shown under the folder list when something in the import already exists at the chosen destination: an item of the same kind with the same name in the same folder. The reader chooses once what happens to all of them.
conflicts.failed: Remoter could not check whether any of this is already in the vault.
conflicts._comment_title: Callout heading. {count} is how many imported items have a namesake at the destination.
conflicts.title: {count, plural, one {# item is already there} other {# items are already there}}
conflicts._comment_item: One line of the list. {name} is the item's name, {path} the vault folder it is in, as 'Production / Web'.
conflicts._comment_policyLabel: Accessible name of the three choices below.
conflicts.policyLabel: What to do with items that are already there
conflicts.keepBothHint: Import them next to the ones already there. Nothing in the vault changes.
conflicts.skipHint: Leave the vault's copies as they are and bring in only what is new.
conflicts._comment_replace: The imported copy overwrites the existing item, passwords included. The warning that it cannot be undone must survive translation.
conflicts.replaceHint: The vault's copies take the imported settings and passwords. This cannot be undone.

commit._comment_: Step 7 — the last screen before anything is written, and the button that writes.
commit.title: Ready to write
commit.lead: This is the step that touches your vault. Everything before it happened in the core's own memory.
commit._comment_into: Heading over the counts. {folder} is either a folder path from the vault or the 'destination.top' phrase.
commit._comment_countSecrets: Passwords that will be encrypted into the vault by this commit.
commit._comment_countExcluded: How many nodes the user unticked in the preview. Two facts in one label: they were unticked, and nothing will be written for them.
commit._comment_commit: The button that writes. Imperative, with the number of nodes it will create.
commit.committing: Writing the import as one transaction…
commit.committingNote: Every node and every sealed password lands together. If anything fails, the vault file is left exactly as it was.
commit._comment_transactionTitle: SECURITY-ADJACENT. The one warning that cannot be given again later: there is no undo, and unticking in the preview is the only remedy that exists before the button is pressed.
commit.transactionBody: Either all of this reaches your vault file or none of it does. Remoter cannot undo an import afterwards, so anything you did not want should be unticked in the preview before you press the button — deleting it from the tree is the only remedy after.
commit.nothing: Nothing is ticked, so there is nothing to write. Go back to the preview and tick something.

result._comment_: Step 8 — what was written. The import is finished and cannot be taken back.
result._comment_title: The heading. {count} nodes are now in the vault.
result.title: {count, plural, one {# item is in your vault} other {# items are in your vault}}
result._comment_lead: {folder} is either a folder path from the vault or the 'destination.top' phrase.
result._comment_refusedTitle: SHOWN ONLY when the parser refused items — items that were in the file and are not in the vault, as opposed to ones the reader unticked. {count} is how many. Do not soften: an import that left part of the file behind is not a success, and this is the last screen the reader sees.
result.refusedTitle: {count, plural, one {# item in the file did not come in} other {# items in the file did not come in}}
result._comment_refusedBody: Follows the heading, above the list of refused items. The advice is deliberate: there is no undo, so importing the corrected file again into the same folder would duplicate everything that did come in.
result.refusedBody: They were in the file and nothing in the vault stands for them. Everything else was written. Correct them in the application they came from and import that file again into a new folder — this import cannot be undone.
result._comment_refusedNotAllListed: Shown under the list when the report stopped growing before the end of the file, so the names of the remaining refusals were never recorded. {count} is how many are missing from the list.
result.refusedNotAllListed: {count, plural, one {# more is not listed here: the report stopped growing before the end of the file.} other {# more are not listed here: the report stopped growing before the end of the file.}}
result._comment_countImported: Labels under the large numbers in the stat tiles. Plain nouns and noun phrases, lower case.
result._comment_countSkipped: Nodes left out because the user unticked them, as opposed to ones the parser refused.
result._comment_rotateTitle: SECURITY-CRITICAL. The passwords just imported came out of a file that protected nothing, so they are already known to anyone who ever had a copy of it. Changing them on the servers is the only fix. Do not soften this heading into 'consider rotating'.
result._comment_rotateDefault: SECURITY-CRITICAL. Used when the file was encrypted with mRemoteNG's published default password.
result.rotateDefault: {count, plural, one {# password came} other {# passwords came}} out of a file encrypted with mRemoteNG's well-known default password. Anyone who has ever held a copy of that file already knows them.
result._comment_rotateLegacy: SECURITY-CRITICAL. Used instead when the file used the legacy AES-CBC scheme.
result.rotateLegacy: {count, plural, one {# password came} other {# passwords came}} out of a file encrypted with the legacy AES-CBC scheme, whose key was an unsalted hash of the password. Anyone who has held a copy of that file could have read them.
result._comment_rotateAfter: SECURITY-CRITICAL. Follows either of the two above. 'They are still the passwords the servers accept' is the whole point: being safe in the vault does not make them safe.
result.rotateAfter: They are safe in the vault now, but they are still the passwords the servers accept. Change them there, then update them here.
result._comment_conflictsTitle: SHOWN ONLY when the import met items the vault already had. The three lines under it appear only when their count is above zero.
result.replaced: {count, plural, one {# item took the imported settings.} other {# items took the imported settings.}}
result.unchanged: {count, plural, one {# item was left as it was.} other {# items were left as they were.}}
result.merged: {count, plural, one {# imported folder went into a folder the vault already had.} other {# imported folders went into folders the vault already had.}}
result.noUndoBody: Remoter cannot take an import back. If this is not what you wanted, delete the imported nodes from the tree — they are together under the folder you chose, which is why choosing one is worth doing.
result._comment_preservedHead: The same section as report.preservedHead, shown again after the commit. Deliberately identical in English: it is the same list, and a reader who saw it on the report should recognise it here. Keep the two in step.
result._comment_preservedNote: Deliberately identical to report.preservedNote. Keep the two in step.
result.preservedNote: Nothing was discarded. If a later version of Remoter learns to read these, they will be there.

discard._comment_: The dialog shown when the user leaves the wizard with a parsed file still held in the core. SECURITY-ADJACENT: what is being dropped is not a screenful of data but the parsed file, with every password it recovered in plaintext. Leaving wipes them, which is the desired outcome — the cost is only that the file would have to be read again.
discard.title: Discard this import?
discard.body: The parsed file is held in the core, along with every password it recovered. Leaving now drops it and wipes them. Nothing has been written to your vault, so there is nothing to undo — but the file would have to be read again.
discard._comment_keep: Imperative: stay in the wizard and carry on.
discard._comment_discard: Imperative: drop the parse and leave the wizard.
discard.failed: The preview could not be dropped.
discard._comment_leaveAnyway: Offered only after dropping the preview failed, so a broken core cannot trap the user in the wizard.
discard.leaveAnywayHint: The core drops a preview when the vault locks, so leaving does not keep it open indefinitely.
